title: New to the UK: can I use the NHS? After paying the IHS, what do I still pay for?
summary: Which NHS services are free in England once you have paid the IHS, which you still pay for, and the situation for visitors who have not paid the IHS and people with settled status.
content:
# New to the UK: can I use the NHS? After paying the IHS, what do I still pay for?

Last updated: 2026-11-27

> This guide mainly covers **England**. Healthcare is run separately in each part of the UK, and the charging rules for prescriptions, dentists and glasses are different in Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland; we will cover them separately.

When you apply for a visa you pay a large IHS charge, so many people naturally assume that healthcare in the UK will then be free. The first time they are charged for a prescription or get a bill from a dentist, they find out that is not the case.

What the IHS actually gives you is "use of the NHS on broadly the same terms as people who live in the UK long term". People who live here pay for some kinds of care, so after paying the IHS you pay for those too. Once you understand this, most of the other questions fall into place.

## What is the IHS, and who pays it?

IHS stands for Immigration Health Surcharge, a healthcare charge paid together with the visa fee when you apply for a visa. In general:

- if you apply from outside the UK for a visa of more than 6 months, you pay it;
- if you apply from inside the UK, you pay it whatever the length;
- you do not pay it for visitor visas, such as for tourism or visiting family, or when applying for settlement;
- some people are exempt, for example Health and Care Worker visa holders and their family members.

You still have to pay the IHS even if you have private medical insurance. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-ihs-who-needs-to-pay)

The charge is paid upfront for the full length of the visa. The current rates are:

- **£776 a year**: students, **students' dependants**, Youth Mobility Scheme visas, and people under 18 when they apply;
- **£1,035 a year**: all other visa applications.

It is important to be clear: the £776 rate is only for students themselves and students' dependants. If you are on a Skilled Worker or spouse visa, your dependants generally pay £1,035, unless they are under 18 when they apply or are exempt. Dependants pay their own IHS when they apply for their visa; they are not "covered" by the main applicant's payment. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-ihs-rates-and-dependants)

## After paying the IHS, what is free?

Once your visa starts, you can use the NHS on IHS terms. However, if the Home Office has not yet made a decision on your visa, you may have to pay for treatment during that time. If you are asked about your status when you get care, people with an electronic immigration status (eVisa) may need to prove it online with a share code. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-ihs-start-date-and-share-code)

After paying the IHS, you use the NHS in much the same way as people who live here:

- **seeing a GP**: consultations are free;
- **A&E**: free;
- **hospital treatment**: including referral to a hospital specialist and staying in hospital, generally with no extra charge. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-ihs-covered-services)

These entitlements follow your visa. When your visa expires, so does this entitlement. If you applied to extend your visa before it expired and are still waiting for a decision, whether you remain exempt during that time depends on whether the extension is eventually granted. Individual situations can be complicated; if you are unsure, ask the hospital's charging staff or check the guidance on GOV.UK. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-ihs-cover-ends-and-in-time-extension)

Whether you pay for hospital treatment in England depends on the charging rules, including ordinary residence and applicable exemptions or reciprocal arrangements. The passport you hold does not by itself establish entitlement. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-entitlement-not-nationality)

## What you still pay for after paying the IHS

GOV.UK says it plainly: after paying the IHS, you still pay for prescriptions, dental treatment, eye tests and assisted conception (fertility treatment). [See the official source](#guide-evidence-ihs-still-pay-for)

### Prescriptions

In England, when your GP gives you a prescription, the pharmacy charges "per item". The charge is currently **£9.90** per item and has been frozen for 2026/27. If one prescription has three medicines on it, you pay three times. Contraception and medicines for hospital inpatients are free. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-prescription-charge-per-item)

Some people get free prescriptions, depending on age, pregnancy or having recently given birth, certain medical conditions, low income and so on. Paying the IHS is not itself a reason for free prescriptions, and students are not automatically exempt because they are students. You can check whether you qualify on the website of NHSBSA (the NHS organisation that handles these charges). [See the official source](#guide-evidence-prescription-exemptions-not-ihs)

If you need several medicines long term, look into a Prescription Prepayment Certificate (PPC), which works like a "season ticket" for prescriptions: £32.05 for 3 months or £114.50 for 12 months. According to NHSBSA, it usually saves money if you need more than 3 prescription items in 3 months, or more than 11 in a year. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-prescription-prepayment-certificate)

### Dentists

This is the one that surprises people most. After paying the IHS, you still pay to see an NHS dentist. NHS dental care in England is charged in bands, and from 1 April 2026 the charges are:

- **Band 1, £27.90**: examination, diagnosis (including X-rays), advice on prevention, and a scale and polish if the dentist thinks it is needed;
- **Band 2, £76.60**: everything in Band 1, plus fillings, root canal treatment, extractions and similar;
- **Band 3, £332.10**: everything in the first two bands, plus crowns, dentures, bridges and similar;
- **urgent dental care, £27.90**. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-nhs-dental-charge-bands)

The people who get free NHS dental treatment are mainly those under 18, those under 19 and still in full-time education, people who are pregnant or have had a baby in the last 12 months, and people who receive certain benefits or have the relevant certificate through the low income scheme. The IHS is not among them; the same applies to students, who pay once they are past that age. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-free-nhs-dental-treatment)

We will write a separate guide on finding an NHS dentist and roughly how much private dentists cost.

### Eye tests

You generally still pay for an eye test after paying the IHS. We have not been able to verify sufficiently reliable information on the cost of glasses and who gets free eye tests, so we do not go into this here. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-eye-tests-charged)

### Assisted conception (IVF and similar)

In England, the free hospital treatment that comes with paying the IHS **does not include** assisted conception services such as IVF. This exception is written explicitly into the rules for England. The rules in Scotland and Wales are different and cannot simply be applied the same way; we will cover them separately. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-assisted-conception-excluded)

## If someone has not paid the IHS, can they not use the NHS at all?

No. Two things are free in England for everyone, whether or not they have paid the IHS and whatever their status:

- **seeing a GP**: anyone can register with a GP and have consultations free of charge;
- **A&E** itself (except for people who came to the UK specifically to get treatment). [See the official source](#guide-evidence-gp-and-ae-free-for-everyone)

The difference is mainly with hospital care. People who have not paid the IHS and are not exempt, such as short-term visitors coming to see family or as tourists, may be charged if they are admitted to hospital from A&E or need to return for follow-up appointments, generally at 150% of the standard NHS rate. However, treatment that is urgent and must be given immediately will not be delayed or refused because the patient cannot pay at that moment. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-visitor-hospital-charges)

People with indefinite leave to remain (ILR, settlement) do not pay the IHS any more and are not charged for hospital care, but they still pay the charges that people who live here pay, such as prescriptions and dental care. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-ilr-holders)

## Which group do visiting parents fall into?

Parents who come on a visitor visa to stay for a few months do not pay the IHS, and do not get the same entitlements just because you have paid it. Seeing a GP and A&E are free for them, but hospital treatment such as admission and follow-up appointments is usually charged. The NHS recommends that visitors have medical or travel insurance for their whole visit. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-visiting-parents-coverage-and-insurance)

There is one more thing to know: if a hospital bill of £500 or more is left unpaid for more than two months after it was issued, with no agreement to pay by instalments, the hospital must report the debt, and it reaches the Home Office. Under the current Immigration Rules, a debt like this can be a reason to refuse a future visa application: it "may" be refused, not that it definitely will be. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-nhs-debt-reporting-and-refusal)

There is a lot to say about parents getting healthcare in the UK, so we will write a separate guide on it.

## What paying the IHS really means

- While your visa is valid, you can use the NHS like someone who lives in the UK long term: GP, A&E and hospital treatment involve no extra charge.
- You pay what people who live here pay: in England, mainly prescriptions, dental care and eye tests.
- In England, assisted conception such as IVF is not covered free of charge by the IHS. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-assisted-conception-excluded)
- Dependants pay their own IHS; the £776 rate is only for students and students' dependants, and dependants on other visas generally pay £1,035.
- Not having paid the IHS does not mean you cannot get care: GP and A&E are generally free for everyone, and the charges apply to follow-on hospital treatment. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-gp-and-ae-free-for-everyone)
- Parents visiting you are not covered by your IHS, so it is best to buy insurance in advance. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-visiting-parents-coverage-and-insurance)
